in the mouse model of P. berghe infection, there is a complex interaction of the host immune response and the parasite, which leads to the development of a number of immunopathological processes, which in turn lead to a high mortality.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cerebral malaria is a multifactorial condition, in which the parasite is the main factor, but the host is also important, as is the immune response, which may be protective or damaging.

cerebral and other tissue changes in this model are associated with a high degree of parasitaemia, and that these lesions may be related to the immunopathological events that occur during the infection.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the immunopathology of malaria is not a single disease but rather a spectrum of diseases.
the immune responses of different mouse strains to P. berghei are not the same, and that this is reflected in the histopathology of different tissues during infection.

the immunopathology of cerebral malaria in mice is similar to that described for human cases, and the model can be used to investigate the pathogenesis of cerebral lesions and to test the effects of potential anti-malarial drugs.
